claims.text: Introducing a hierarchical microstructure through heat treatment can improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed intervention can start from an as-cast or solution-treated high-entropy alloy.
A combination of high-temperature annealing and water quenching can induce a hierarchical microstructure.
The hypothesis should hold during high-temperature testing up to 1000°C at controlled strain rates.
The induced hierarchical microstructure contains nanoscale disordered FCC particles inside ordered L12 precipitates.
The hierarchical microstructure acts as an array of obstacles that pins superdislocations.
Pinning of superdislocations increases the energy required for dislocation motion.
The proposed impediment to dislocation motion enhances high-temperature yield strength.
The proposed impediment to dislocation motion enhances toughness.
The hierarchical alloy will have greater high-temperature yield strength than a conventional high-entropy alloy without the hierarchical microstructure.
The hierarchical alloy will have greater high-temperature ductility than a conventional high-entropy alloy without the hierarchical microstructure.
Higher high-temperature yield strength and ductility represent improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss.
The appropriate baseline is a conventional high-entropy alloy without a hierarchical microstructure.
The benefit of the hierarchical microstructure may be limited by the thermal stability of its nanoscale disordered FCC particles.
The optimal heat-treatment protocol is not fully understood.
The mechanisms governing formation and stability of the hierarchical microstructure are not fully understood.
